body:
You are an editor tightening DIALOGUE TEXT for a video game. Reply in plain text only, in exactly the format asked at the end.

"The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG (think Baldur's Gate 3: fully voiced, branching dialogue). It is folk horror in Wickermoor, a village in an afterlife realm of endless autumn night; deadpan humour beside real dread. These are the village's conversations. Players say the village is a WALL OF TALK: too many words before anything happens. Your job is to make every line shorter and sharper, the way a good film editor cuts a scene, without losing anything that matters.

FOR EACH NUMBERED LINE answer one of:
- `n => KEEP` when the line is already tight (most lines of 15 words or fewer should be KEEP).
- `n => new text` with the tightened line. Aim for about half to two thirds of the old length. Cut throat-clearing, repetition of what the line or the line before already said, stacked adjectives, second examples, flavour that leads nowhere, and explanations the listener doesn't need.
- `n => CUT` only for a line whose content is entirely repeated by another line in the same conversation node (shown in [brackets]); never for a line that is the only one of its node, never for an interject line, never for the first line of a node.

WHAT MUST SURVIVE in every line you tighten: every name, place, item, number, price, time, clue, hint, secret, warning, threat, promise and joke punchline; the speaker's voice and quirks (a mayor's pomposity, a constable's few words, a poet's floweriness, a child's simplicity, a country drawl in word choice); the mood. If a line does two jobs, keep both. Never add new facts. Keep `{name}` exactly as it is wherever it appears. Keep the line in the same person and tense.

NARRATOR lines (speaker Narrator, the Vagrant telling the tale: folksy, warm, wry Southern drawl in word choice) stay second person, present tense, one or two sentences, concrete senses, no game words, never "suddenly".

STYLE: plain punctuation; straight quotes; no em dashes, asterisks, brackets or stage directions; do not use -> or => inside the text.

## The lines

### morgan.dialogue
645. [secret_ok] morgan: Funny thing, the clock strikes one bell and when I blink it is striking the next. I woke here small and alone, and the years between still slip through my fingers.
646. [secret_fail] Narrator: Morgan gently closes the stained ledger under a bundle of dried chamomile.
647. [secret_fail] morgan: Do not mind my messy handwriting, nobody in the hollow can read apothecary scrawl anyway.

### mori.dialogue
648. [start] Narrator: The parlor smells of beeswax and cold tin. Mori pulls open a shallow cedar drawer filled with gleaming brass coffin plates.
649. [start] mori_shade: Forgive the clutter, friends. I stencil these for the Order of the Oak, though the folks named on them are still walking the streets.
650. [who] mori_shade: I truly could not say. On the first of each month, a folded slip and a silver piece wait beneath my door.
651. [who] mori_shade: A man must keep his fires lit, so I oil my punches and I do not watch the threshold.
652. [list] Narrator: Five brass plates lie nested in black velvet, each stamped with neat, square letters.
653. [list] mori_shade: Geneva Fairchild, Howie Butterman, Ambrose Quill, and Finneas Trout. The fifth plate was ordered polished, but left completely blank.
654. [decide] mori_shade: My hands shake more with every letter I strike. You are strangers here, unburdened by our customs: tell me what ought to be done.
655. [warn] Narrator: Word travels the cobbled lanes faster than mist off the moor, leaving shuttered windows and bolted doors behind it.
656. [warn] mori_shade: They cross the mud to avoid my shop now, whispering that the undertaker wishes them cold. Perhaps they are right to fear me.
657. [burn] Narrator: Brass curls and blackens in the belly of the iron stove, filling the small room with a sharp, metallic tang.
658. [burn] mori_shade: Let them come for their silver if they dare. My lungs feel clear for the first hour in a year.
659. [doris] Narrator: Constable Squire turns the paper over once in her gloved fingers, her face as grey and unreadable as slate.
660. [doris] doris_squire: Keep your shop shuttered after the third bell, Mori. I will copy these into the ledger and walk the Round myself.
661. [silent] Narrator: The drawer slides shut with a soft wooden click, swallowing the faint gleam of brass.
662. [silent] mori_shade: Best to let the village sleep easy, I suppose. I will have the oil lamp trimmed before the next slip arrives.
663. [later] Narrator: A single brass plate rests upon the workbench, newly struck, the metal filings still clinging to the letters.
664. [later] mori_shade: The monthly note came while you were at that dreadful house, friends. They finally gave me a name for the blank plate, and I thought you should see it.

### mori_shade.dialogue
665. [start] Narrator: The scent of dried rosemary and freshly turned peat clings to the woman in black. Her white hair gleams like bone under the lantern light.
666. [start] mori_shade: Step softly, newly arrived. You stand upon ground that has welcomed many before you, and will hold many more before the moon wanes.
667. [about_work] mori_shade: When a companion falls in Druskenvald, the soil does not easily let them go. I wash the brow, fold the hands, and pay the earth its proper due.
668. [about_work] mori_shade: Old Yorgrim down at the cemetery taught me the spade-work when I first woke here. Every soul deserves a quiet pillow, whatever they were before.
669. [about_village] mori_shade: The Mayor's folk feed the Oak of Many Faces with blood, while the Brightsingers try to sing the dark away. I keep to the Strangers' way: we owe the Ferryman a polite nod and a clean ledger.
670. [shop_open] mori_shade: Tell me whose memory we are tending, and we shall see them properly laid to rest.
671. [rumour] mori_shade: Do not pluck the white violets that grow round the base of the Founder's Round. Their roots drink deep from those who died without a name, and they weep on your fingers.
672. [check_ok] Narrator: She touches the tarnished brass oar pinned to her lapel, her voice dropping to the hush of river reeds.
673. [check_ok] mori_shade: You know the Vagrant's mark, then. He rowed us all across the dark water once, and he watches still to see if we waste the second breath he gave us.
674. [check_fail] mori_shade: It is only an old keepsake from the riverbank, traveller. A reminder that every road ends at the water's edge.
675. [raising] Narrator: The parlor goes awful still save for the dry rustle of pages as she turns to a black ledger on the desk, smellin' of cedar and cold tallow.
676. [raising] mori_shade: I do not call the departed back myself. I only go down to the water, ask the Ferryman to turn his oar, and carry him his toll.
677. [raising] mori_shade: He turns his oar only for souls in the water no more than ten days. They return weak and stumbling for ten days, the water's shadow clinging on.
678. [raising] mori_shade: The toll is a thousand gold pieces for each soul I carry to him, whoever they were and however far they came. I keep no gems and ask no other payment.
679. [raising] mori_shade: You will see the toll set out for each companion before anything is paid. Tell me whom you mean to call back to the near shore.
680. [raising_after] mori_shade: The Ferryman keeps his ledger open, and the offer stands for the full ten days, whenever your purse allows.
681. [raising_closed] Narrator: The lamps burn low in the parlor, and a damp chill settles deep into the quiet room at this hour.
682. [raising_closed] mori_shade: The Midnight and Witching hours I give to the graves, and the Ferryman takes no asking now.
683. [raising_closed] mori_shade: Come back to me from the Twilight Hour until the Evening Hour is spent. The ten days will keep.

### mrs_oakum.dialogue
684. [start] Narrator: The tang of cold tallow and wet dog hangs about her apron. She keeps her head down, paring grey fat from a knucklebone with a notched knife.
685. [start] mrs_oakum: If you want prime cuts, talk to the master up front. I only scrape the troughs and haul the bone-bucket out back.
686. [menu] mrs_oakum: Speak quick if you need something. The clock don't wait on idle tongues.
687. [work] mrs_oakum: It suits me fine. Folks leave me be, and I get the gristle and marrow-ends to carry home before the Evening bell rings.
688. [work] mrs_oakum: Once that bell tolls, I lock myself out on the high scrub till Twilight comes round.
689. [village] mrs_oakum: Folk here pray to their big thirsty tree and think the hedges will keep the dark out. A fence only keeps in what wants to stay.
690. [rumour] mrs_oakum: Something foul is seeping out of the Skitterdeep mine, up north-west in the crags. The creek water tastes of copper and bad fever, and the beasts know it.
691. [secret_ok] Narrator: Coarse grey hairs bristle along the scarred skin of her forearms, and her breath catches at the scent of raw liver on the block.
692. [secret_ok] mrs_oakum: Keep your eyes to yourself, stranger. A heavy chain and a sack of butcher's offal is all that keeps my teeth out of this town come dark.
693. [secret_fail] mrs_oakum: Best not stare at a working woman's hands while she holds a cleaver, friend. Mind your own business.

### myrtle_somerton.dialogue
694. [start] Narrator: She smells of starch and dried chamomile, her hands folded neat over her apron while her gaze flicks toward the nursery stairs.
695. [start] myrtle_somerton: Good evening. If you are looking for Wendel, he keeps his hours in the office, though I ask that you keep your voices low near little Rose's door.
696. [about_work] myrtle_somerton: Being the mayor's wife means keeping the silver bright and making sure Wendel does not promise the parish away to flatter quality. My real work is keeping Rose at her lessons and indoors.
697. [about_village] myrtle_somerton: It is a respectable village when folk mind their own hearths. I tell Wendel that all this fuss over old trees and midnight bells only gives the simple folk bad dreams.
698. [rumour] myrtle_somerton: Too many shutters have stayed barred past the third bell this month. The baker's apprentice has a rattle in his chest that no kettle of broth seems to touch.
699. [secret_ok] Narrator: Her knuckles whiten on her apron hem, and you see iron pins driven into the windowsill beside a child's wooden doll.
700. [secret_ok] myrtle_somerton: People do not just wander off into the gorse when they know the paths from birth, no matter what the constable writes down. I bolt Rose's shutters before the first bell, and I do not open them for anyone.
701. [secret_fail] Narrator: She smooths her skirt with a brisk pat and offers a tight, proper nod.
702. [secret_fail] myrtle_somerton: A mother is always careful in damp weather, that is all. The moor air is hard on small lungs.

### oak.dialogue
703. [start] Narrator: Dark sap weeps from the knots of the old oak as a dozen wooden eyelids creak open in the moonlight. The smell of iron and wet earth rises from the roots, and the carved mouths begin to move together.
704. [listen] Narrator: A dry chorus rustles through the bark like dead leaves scraping across a stone floor. They whisper that their roots are parched, that they are so very tired of the dark, and that the axe took them for crimes they never did.
705. [listen] Narrator: Wooden teeth click together in a ragged plea: cut the boughs, split the heartwood, and let us out.
706. [names] Narrator: Three faces near the base of the trunk strain forward against the grain, speaking one after another in hushed, splintered breaths. A hollow-cheeked woman claims she only took a loaf of barley bread, while a gaunt man swears the boundary stone was moved before he ever plowed the field.

## Reply format
One line per numbered line above (62 lines, 645 to 706), in order, exactly `n => text`, `n => KEEP` or `n => CUT`. No quotes around the text, no commentary.
